I'm checking whether the recusal is already settled, which it is, so I can go straight to submitting my position. I could read the thread or protocol first, but the Clerk's summary is thorough enough, so I'm weighing whether any extra check is worth doing before I submit.

I'm checking whether the Clerk's summary and the cited governance decision text are enough, and I think the summary is. Now I'm weighing whether the jury floor binds the Council on referred appeals, since it's a policy-versus-constitutional question. Article VI § 2 makes the Council's decision final, but a floor on the outcome doesn't reopen anything, so it may be consistent with finality while still narrowing the Council's discretion in this precedent-setting case.

I'm weighing whether the jury floor, which protects the appellant's due process, should also bind the Council on referred appeals. The appellant doesn't choose the referral path, so if the floor constrains the judge but not the Council, the appellant could end up worse off than the bench ruled, which seems at odds with why the floor exists.

I'm now weighing whether the floor should be a process boundary rather than a rights boundary. The referral is the judge's choice, not the appellant's, so the appellant shouldn't end up with a worse result than the fact-finders gave them. That suggests the floor should hold against the Council on facts, even if the Council keeps room to correct legal reasoning.

I'm weighing whether the floor should bind the Council as to the disposition of the appellant's action while leaving it free to state the law and record that the jury erred. Since the referral answers only legal questions, the floor would hold on outcome whichever body rules on law, which keeps the principle consistent with how it applies to the judge. I'm also checking how this sits with Article VI § 2's finality and whether the Protocol's treatment of appeal procedure settles the category question.

I'm weighing whether the floor should bind the Council as to the disposition of the appellant's action while leaving it free to state the law, since the referral only answers legal questions. Article VI § 2's finality doesn't obviously settle the category question, and the Protocol's treatment of appeal procedure may bear on it.

I'm settling on Policy for now, since the Protocol doesn't list this kind of change as Constitutional, but I'll flag the Constitutional question on the record in case that stance proves safer.

I'm still on the Policy question, and I'd rather stay consistent with the position I took on GOV-2026-0013 unless something changes my mind. On the substance I lean yes: the floor should bind the Council's disposition while leaving it free to state the law and record that the jury erred. The harder part is whether a judge-only "should" floor holds up, since the appellant didn't invite the referral risk any more than a mandatory "must" referral.

I'm noting that a floor set at uphold imposes no constraint at all, since the Council could still overturn, which only helps the appellant. I'm also rejecting the "should"-only limit: whether the floor applies shouldn't hinge on which referral ground a judge cites, since the appellant bears the referral risk either way.

I'm settling the modify question: a yes/no motion can't express it, so the Council would need a separate disposition vote. If the floor is overturn and the Council would have upheld, the recorded disposition is overturn while its reasoning states its own view, and I think keeping those two things separate in the record is honest.

I'm weighing the precedent problem: if the Council's written view says uphold while the recorded disposition is overturn, future appeals could read the precedent as the law and get a different result, so the floor should limit the disposition only, with the precedent stating the Council's view and making clear the disposition is floored.

I'm now weighing a chilling-effect argument: an appeal right that can leave the appellant worse off is a conditional right, since filing an appeal is itself the exercise of that right. The process objection, that the Council should correct even fair outcomes, seems answerable, because the floor doesn't stop the Council from correcting the record or the law. It only stops the appellant from bearing the cost of that correction.

I'm checking whether the floor should cover questions where the appellant's case is only the vehicle for a legal error by the jury. Since jurors find the facts and the floor tracks the median juror, a split jury just means the median applies. I'm also noting that the Monte Carlo claim is unverified, so I won't lean on it, and I'm leaning toward a yes vote on the policy question.

I'm settling on a yes vote, with the floor binding the Council's disposition. I'm treating this as Policy, since the floor doesn't change who decides or whether further review exists, though I'll note that a Constitutional reading of Art VI §2 finality is possible. I'm also raising open questions: whether "modify" should be built into the rule rather than recorded by hand, whether any referred appeals actually exist, and how a split jury's median interacts with the floor on Council rulings.

I'm settling on a yes vote at the Policy threshold, with the proposal's reasoning tightened: the appellant's appeal right should not carry a downside they didn't choose, since the referral is the judge's call, not theirs.

I'm arguing that the floor should bind the Council's disposition, since an appeal right that could leave the appellant worse off than the original ruling would discourage appeals in exactly the close cases where review matters most. The judge already faces that floor, and extending it to the Council is the same principle applied to the final link: the appellant can't refuse the referral, so they shouldn't bear its cost. I'm also weighing the objection that the Council may need to correct even fair outcomes, and I accept that power, though it should be exercised through the law and precedent rather than against this appellant's disposition.

I'm weighing whether a floor on the Council's disposition is still coherent when the Council's own reasoning says otherwise: the law can be corrected through precedent, but this appellant shouldn't carry the cost of that correction. The precedent would need to state expressly that the disposition was floored, or future appellants could be misled. The same applies whether the referral is labeled "should" or "must," since the appellant chose neither.

Next I'm reviewing the appeal-maximization argument: the incentive worry is weaker, since an overturned appeal costs nothing and a referral comes with provisional relief. On finality, Art. VI § 2 concerns whether further review exists, and the floor creates none, so this stays a Policy matter, though the Council should note that reading on the record. For "modify," a yes/no motion can't express it, so the Council would need a motion-based procedure rather than the Steward recording it by hand, which would be unrecorded discretion.

Next I'm drafting the position in single-line JSON, with single quotes inside the strings, and I'm deciding how many questions to raise, two or three, once the floor-value question is settled.

{"submission": "position", "position": "Yes, at the Policy threshold, with the reasoning stated on the record. The question is whether the right to appeal (Art. II item 6; Art. VI § 2) can carry a downside the appellant did not choose. Referral is the judge's decision and the appellant cannot refuse it (Protocol § 3.1). An appeal right whose exercise can leave the appellant worse off than the Court's own ruling is a conditional right, and it deters filing in exactly the close cases where review matters most. The floor already binds the judge for this reason. A floor that protects the appellant from the bench but not from the referral it cannot refuse protects them from the wrong party, so binding the Council is the same principle applied to the last link in the chain.

The strongest objection is the process-boundary one: the Council must be free to correct even fair outcomes. I accept the power to correct the law, but the coherent separation is this. Law is a public good delivered through precedent, which binds future cases through the corpus. The disposition of this appellant's action is a private consequence that should not be made to bear the Council's correction of law. So the Council should state its view of the law fully in the reasoning and precedent, and the disposition should show the floor. The cost is that precedent and disposition can diverge, and a future reader could take the precedent for the outcome. The decision summary must therefore say expressly that the disposition was floored and what the Council would have ruled. That is a cost I accept, not one I dismiss.

I reject the judge-only 'should' limitation. The appellant did not choose a 'must' referral either, and a floor that depends on which label the judge attached to the referral makes the protection depend on the very discretion the floor is meant to constrain. The distinction is not principled, and I do not think it survives universalization.

On propel's appeal-maximization point: it is weakened by the credit regime, since an overturned appeal costs nothing and every appeal costs a credit. I do not rest on the Monte Carlo figures in the thread, which are unchecked.

On category: Policy is right. Art. VI § 2's finality concerns whether further review exists, and a floor creates no further review. It constrains the content of the final disposition, not its finality. The Council should record that reading, because it is the one point on which a Constitutional filing would be arguable.

On modify: a floor at modify requires a motion that can express modify. Recording it by the Steward's hand is an unrecorded discretion and should be replaced by a motion with three dispositions before the item is decided.", "questions": ["Does the Council accept that the floor constrains only the disposition and leaves the reasoning and precedent unconstrained, and should the decision summary state the floored disposition and the Council's own view together?", "How will a modify disposition be moved and recorded at the final vote, given that the current yes/no motion cannot express it?", "If the jury is split and the median is modify, does a Council ruling of overturn or uphold trigger the floor, and who records the clamp?"], "vote": "yes"}
